cases.body:
# Leave room for the repaired bowl

## Position

I like the cracked blue bowl more than the polished pieces beside it. Its label says the maker repaired it twice, which is a better invitation to look closely than another date in bold type. That preference is why I am wary of treating a museum label as a machine for delivering facts. Visitors should be able to find the basics, but I do not want clarity to become an excuse for sanding the objects smooth. This memo asks whether a small layout change deserves a longer trial, not whether stories should give way to checklists.

## Evidence

In the classroom session, 27 of 36 participants located the accession number within 30 seconds. The redesigned label therefore improved visitors' understanding of the collection by 75 percent. I have written that second sentence more confidently than the exercise warrants. Locating a number is useful, but it is not the same task as explaining why a repaired bowl matters. I also do not know how these participants would have done with the old layout. I want a label that opens a door, not one that hustles people through it. The evaluation should help me ask a narrower question without making the number disappear just because it is inconvenient to explain.

## Recommendation

My recommendation is to keep both label versions for a short comparison before replacing the gallery labels. I would ask visitors what they noticed as well as whether they found the accession number. A fast answer can be useful without being the only answer worth collecting. The bowl's repairs should still have room in the story. That is the part of the proposal I am least willing to trade away, even if a cleaner spreadsheet would be easier to present at the committee meeting.

cases.body:
# Keep the notebook's tenses straight

## Question

The seed envelopes have more handwriting than seeds in some years. I want the garden group to keep that uneven record rather than pretend every tray was part of a designed experiment. The March result from lot Alder is worth reporting because someone counted it, not because it settles the best way to germinate every stored seed. My question is what we can responsibly say from that record and what a better next test could ask. Those are related questions, but they belong in different tenses.

## Record and next test

The March record reported 8 germinations among 40 seeds from lot Alder after 14 days. The March test randomly assigned seeds to soaking and no-soaking groups, proving soaking improved germination. I want to keep the count because it is the observation we actually have, but my explanation of the method needs checking. The record at this address has since changed, and I do not want the newer page to make the old notebook entry vanish. For June, I propose randomly assigning seeds from one lot to soaking and no-soaking groups, then using the same observation period for both. That last sentence is a proposal. It should not quietly become a description of what the volunteers already did.

## Closing

I would put the old result and the new protocol on separate pages in the shared notebook. That is not bureaucratic tidiness to me. It gives the next volunteer a fair chance of knowing which statement is an observation and which is an invitation to try something. If the June comparison never happens, the March count should still be readable, and the proposed method should still be marked as a plan. A careful record can admit unfinished work without apologizing for it.
